analysis.one_liner: Wipes out EPA's 2011 toxic-air limits on industrial boilers and incinerators, then delays replacements for years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and died when the 112th Congress ended, leaving the 2011 boiler emission rules in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would void four EPA rules issued in March 2011 that limit hazardous air pollution, including mercury, dioxins, and fine particles, from industrial, commercial, and institutional boilers and from commercial and industrial solid waste incinerators. It orders EPA to write replacement rules within 15 months, bars compliance deadlines sooner than five years after a rule takes effect, and requires EPA to pick the least burdensome option it is allowed to pick. It also publishes a list of fuels, including coal waste, tire-derived fuel, and many biomass and industrial byproducts, that could not be treated as solid waste, which would keep them out of the stricter incinerator rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Operators of the thousands of large boilers and incinerators covered by the rules, especially energy-intensive manufacturers, pulp and paper mills, and institutions such as hospitals and universities, would avoid or postpone expensive retrofits of pollution controls and get compliance dates set with cost and employment factors written into law.

how_it_helps.text: The four March 2011 EPA rules, including the major- and area-source boiler standards and the commercial and industrial solid waste incinerator standards, would have no force or effect, as though they had never taken effect.

EPA would have to issue replacement rules within 15 months, and compliance dates for any new standards could be no earlier than five years after the rules' effective date, considering costs, feasibility, equipment availability, and potential net employment impacts.
EPA would be required to impose the least burdensome regulatory alternative for each replacement rule and to ensure standards can be met under actual operating conditions.

EPA would have to publish a list of nonhazardous secondary materials that are not solid waste when burned for energy recovery, including coal refuse, coal combustion residuals, tire-derived fuel, creosote-treated wood, and a long list of industrial byproducts, keeping those fuels out of the stricter solid waste incineration standards.

analysis.who_pays: People living near and downwind of the affected boilers and incinerators would keep breathing the mercury, dioxins, and fine particle pollution the 2011 rules were written to cut, for at least the delay period and possibly much longer under weaker replacement standards. The health costs of that exposure fall on nearby residents, not on the facilities emitting it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near boiler and incinerator pollution

drawbacks.text: The bill would strike down final, health-based emission standards that had already completed the Clean Air Act rulemaking process, and replace them through a slower process with a built-in five-year minimum before facilities had to comply.

The statutory fuel list would remove many industrial waste streams, including coal refuse and treated wood, from the stricter incinerator rules by declaring them fuels rather than solid waste, limiting EPA's ability to regulate how they are burned.

Supporters' good-faith case was that the 2011 rules were expensive and technically difficult to meet on schedule for a wide range of facilities, and the bill's stated purpose was to give EPA time to issue 'achievable' standards; the cost an honest supporter accepts is continued toxic emissions from these facilities during the delay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings go to a specific set of facility operators in the form of deferred retrofit costs, while the costs are diffuse health risks borne by people near and downwind of those facilities. Because the bill not only delays but voids final rules and directs EPA to the least burdensome option, the replacement standards would likely be weaker than the ones it wipes out. Supporters' argument about unrealistic compliance timelines has some force, but the bill's structure goes well beyond extra time.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the same day, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Susan Collins introduced S. 1392 on July 20, 2011, joined by original cosponsors including Senators Wyden, Alexander, Landrieu, Toomey, and Pryor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further action of any kind after that referral.
Forty-one senators cosponsored the bill, 29 Republicans and 12 Democrats, but it never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the March 2011 emission standards for boilers and incinerators remained in force, and the operators who would have avoided compliance did not get the relief the bill offered. Communities exposed to boiler and incinerator pollution are better off than they would have been had it passed.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship looked bipartisan, with 41 cosponsors split 29 Republicans and 12 Democrats, but the bill died without a vote in a committee chaired by a Democrat, so no roll calls show how support would have held up.

industries.industry: Industrial, commercial, and institutional boiler operators
industries.note: The bill voids their binding emission limits and pushes any replacement standards back at least five years, letting them defer costly pollution-control retrofits. The deferred cost shows up as continued mercury, dioxin, and particle exposure for nearby and downwind communities.

The bill writes a statutory list of materials, from coal refuse to tire-derived fuel to treated wood, that EPA may not treat as solid waste, permanently keeping those fuels in the lighter regulation of boilers rather than the stricter incinerator standards.

Voiding the standards and delaying compliance shrinks the market for scrubbers, filters, and other controls these facilities would have installed. Their loss comes with the same public exposure to pollution the bill prolongs.
